title: COP31 timeline: How the world got here and what's at stake in Türkiye
content: The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP 31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) will take place from November 9 to November 20, 2026 in Antalya, Turkey. Turkey will host the summit and lead the presidency's action agenda, while Australia, as co-president, will lead the negotiations. At COP31, the Belém Mission will present its report on putting national climate plans into action. The new leadership has also pledged to bring Pacific island nations into focus. Several key issues will be up for negotiation, including adaptation, mitigation, just transition and climate finance. The presidency's action agenda also includes several priorities, notably a proposed global electrification target of 35 per cent by 2035. Here are some major milestones in the history of international climate negotiations. The formation of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in 1988 was a significant milestone. In 1990, the IPCC published its first assessment report. It concluded that global temperatures had risen by 0.3–0.6°C over the previous century and called for an international treaty to address greenhouse gas emissions. This was followed by the adoption of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) in 1992, aimed at tackling greenhouse gas emissions and addressing climate change. In 1995, parties to the UNFCCC held the first Conference of the Parties (COP1) in Berlin. The meeting produced the Berlin Mandate, which called for negotiations on stronger emissions commitments. In 1997, COP3 marked a historic milestone with the adoption of the Kyoto Protocol, the first international treaty to set legally binding greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets for developed countries. The agreement reflected the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, under which developed countries were expected to take the lead because of their greater historical contribution to greenhouse gas emissions. In 2001, at the resumed sixth climate summit in Bonn, governments reached a broad political agreement on the rules for implementing the Kyoto Protocol. On February 16, 2005, the Kyoto Protocol entered into force without the United States, one of the world's largest historical emitters. The treaty had met the requirement for ratification by at least 55 countries, including industrialised countries accounting for at least 55 per cent of their combined 1990 carbon dioxide emissions. In 2009, at COP15 in Copenhagen, the United States, European Union and BASIC countries sought to advance an international climate agreement based on national pledges rather than legally binding emissions reduction targets. The talks exposed deep divisions between developed and developing countries. In 2010, COP16 in Cancún failed to establish new binding emissions targets but agreed to establish the Green Climate Fund. The fund was intended to help developing countries reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. In 2013, at COP19 in Warsaw, delegates from developing countries walked out of discussions over the lack of progress on loss and damage caused by climate change. A compromise agreement eventually established the Warsaw International Mechanism for Loss and Damage. By 2015, global average temperatures had risen to around 1°C above pre-industrial levels. That year, COP21 delivered the Paris Agreement, a landmark global climate treaty. It required developed and developing countries to submit increasingly ambitious climate plans, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). Countries also agreed to hold the rise in global average temperatures to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit warming to 1.5°C. In 2018, young climate activists, including Greta Thunberg, drew global attention to climate change through protests and demonstrations. In 2020, the annual climate summit was postponed because of the Covid-19 pandemic. The United States formally withdrew from the Paris Agreement under then-President Donald Trump. In 2021, at COP26, the Glasgow Climate Pact called for a phasedown of unabated coal power and finalised rules for international carbon trading under the Paris Agreement. The United States also rejoined the Paris Agreement under President Joe Biden. In 2022, COP27 in Egypt delivered a historic agreement to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries deal with the consequences of climate-related disasters. In 2023, COP28 in Dubai operationalised the loss and damage fund and laid the groundwork for negotiations on a new collective quantified goal on climate finance. In November 2025, countries gathered in Belém, Brazil, for COP30. Brazil described it as the implementation COP, but negotiations were marked by disagreements over finance, trade and emissions reductions. Several decisions remained unresolved until the final stages. One of the biggest disappointments concerned fossil fuels. More than 80 countries, rising to 88 by the end of the summit, supported a roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels. However, the final agreement did not explicitly mention fossil fuels. Instead, Brazil announced separate roadmaps on fossil fuels and deforestation outside the formal negotiations. There were some other outcomes. A new two-year programme on climate finance was established to maintain pressure on developed countries to deliver the funding promised at COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. That agreement included a goal of mobilising at least $300 billion annually for developing countries by 2035, alongside a broader ambition to scale climate finance to $1.3 trillion a year. Countries also agreed to triple adaptation finance by 2035. However, developing countries had sought a 2030 deadline, and the baseline for calculating the increase remained unclear. A set of 59 indicators was adopted to track global progress on adaptation, although last-minute changes weakened the outcome. Countries also agreed to establish a just transition mechanism, a key demand from civil society organisations, and adopted a new gender action plan. Two initiatives were launched in Belém: the Belém Mission to 1.5°C and the Global Implementation Accelerator. Both aim to help countries translate their climate commitments into action. Whether governments deliver on those promises at home remains to be seen.

title: Scaling up climate and health measures could prevent 1.56 million deaths annually: WHO
content: Scaling up six climate and health interventions could prevent 1.56 million deaths and 16.67 billion tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions annually, according to WHO. The measures could generate $3.92 trillion in annual economic welfare benefits and $5.44 trillion in fiscal benefits. Five interventions with measurable costs could deliver an estimated $24 in benefits for every $1 invested. Heat-health warning systems offer the highest return on investment, generating an estimated $835 in benefits for every $1 spent. More efficient fossil fuel pricing, including removing inefficient subsidies, could deliver the largest overall economic gains, with substantial benefits for low- and middle-income countries. Scaling up six climate and health interventions worldwide could prevent an estimated 1.56 million deaths annually, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and generate trillions of dollars in economic benefits, according to a new World Health Organization (WHO) report. The report, Global benefits and costs of prioritized actions on climate change and health , estimated that implementing the measures globally could prevent 16.67 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions each year. It also projected annual economic welfare benefits of about $3.92 trillion and fiscal benefits of $5.44 trillion, largely driven by policies to price fossil fuels more efficiently. The analysis examined six interventions: heat-health warning systems, climate-resilient drinking water, basic sanitation, hand hygiene, cleaner household energy and fiscal policies to improve fossil fuel pricing. Together, these measures could deliver three benefits: improved public health, lower emissions and stronger economies. "The climate crisis is a health crisis, but much of the harm it causes can be prevented with tools we already have," said WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. He said scaling up proven interventions could save lives, particularly in countries facing the greatest health risks, and urged governments to place health at the centre of climate negotiations.

title: Climate change is undermining our health and the burden falls heaviest on women
content: Climate change is exacerbating health issues globally, with women in the Pacific disproportionately affected due to food and water insecurity. Chronic diseases like diabetes and heart disease are rising, and women are leading innovative climate solutions. COP31 must prioritise health equity, gender-responsive policies, and accelerated emissions reduction to address these challenges effectively. As sea levels creep higher in the Pacific, salt leaches into the soil , and reduces the land available to grow food. Ocean warming is damaging coral reefs, reducing fish stocks, and salinity has tainted fresh water supplies. As a result, Pacific communities are being forced to turn to imported food , which is often high in calories but low in nutrients. And this, along with a myriad of intersecting social, cultural, and economic factors, has led to a rise in the rates of chronic diseases, such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease . Ahead of the upcoming UN climate conference COP31, discussions by government ministers, civil society advocates, multilateral agencies, and academics at the pre-COP meeting in Fiji and Tuvalu last month emphasised the importance of health for those on the front line of the climate crisis. Women in the Pacific are disproportionately responsible for family care, and the burden of food and water insecurity falls most heavily on their shoulders . Women at the pre-COP meeting told us replanting crops after extreme weather is increasing their domestic burden, contributing to exhaustion and mental ill-health . But these women are not passive bystanders. Again and again in Fiji we heard incredible stories of women developing and implementing their own climate solutions. Australia can learn from their leadership and make health a central part of the global agenda at COP31 . This year’s summit is being promoted as the “ implementation COP ”: acting on existing promises (rather than making new ones) to keep the critical threshold of 1.5°C of warming within reach. There will be a push to increase climate finance – funding for activities to mitigate or adapt to the impacts of climate change. But health needs to be higher up the agenda. Global warming is worsening chronic diseases such as heart disease, stroke, diabetes and cancer, which are the primary cause of death and disability, both in the Pacific and globally . As an amplifier of inequity, it is women who bear the greatest health burden . The Pacific has the highest rates of these chronic diseases in the world. They are responsible for 87 per cent of deaths in the Western Pacific region , with mortality rates in Kiribati five times those of Singapore, and yet they have largely absent from the wider COP agenda. Throughout the pre-COP talks, Pacific leaders repeatedly emphasised the need for climate action to reflect the everyday health realities facing communities. Too often, conversations focus on disasters and emergencies and the acute injuries and infectious disease outbreaks that ensue. The less visible ways climate change is undermining population health are often overlooked. Chronic disease prevention and treatment is shaped by interwoven systems, such as food, water, housing, gender equity and economic security. But policies designed to support the systems are fragmented across sectors and institutions. There was a welcome focus on gender and women’s health at the Fiji meeting, including discussions about how extreme heat is making pregnancy more dangerous for mothers , and women are facing poorer health outcomes and heightened care giving. Tuvalu prime minister Feleti Teo said it best: Ensuring that gender and health are fully integrated into climate financing is not just an ambition; it is an urgent necessity for the survival and wellbeing of our island communities. Fortunately, many Pacific Island nations are making inroads at addressing these challenges. The Pacific Resilience Facility , a climate finance mechanism owned and led by Pacific people, is funding women-led climate projects, such as installing community water tanks. One community leader at pre-CoP spoke about the value of having a clean and reliable water supply for their village in remote Fiji for the first time, for the modest cost of US6,000(A8,600). Projects like this demonstrate climate adaptation can drive health and economic development that creates broader prosperity. Other changes that should be reflected at the COP31 meetings in Turkey include: 1. chronic diseases should be included in national climate and health action plans 2. climate action must include strengthening primary health care 3. climate action must be gender-responsive, with women included in climate leadership 4. most importantly, emissions reduction must be accelerated to keep 1.5°C within reach. The Pacific has shown the world what climate leadership looks like. Now the priorities discussed at Fiji must be taken up at COP31. Climate change is multi-faceted and our response must be the same; connecting climate action, health equity and sustainable development. Veronica Le Nevez , Co-Director, Impact and Engagement, The George Institute for Global Health, George Institute for Global Health and Laura Emily Downey , Associate professor, George Institute for Global Health This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. title: $305 billion needed, $28 billion delivered: Developing countries face massive climate adaptation funding gap
content: Developing countries need $305 billion annually for climate adaptation, a figure that could rise to $420 billion by 2035. Even tripling international public adaptation finance would meet only 20–29% of funding needs by 2035. International public adaptation finance reached an estimated $28.2–31.7 billion in 2024, far below requirements. Limited funding and barriers to accessing finance continue to hamper adaptation efforts in vulnerable countries and communities. Developing countries need an estimated $305 billion annually to adapt to climate change, but even a tripling of international public adaptation finance could meet only 20-29 per cent of their requirements by 2035, according to a new United Nations report. The annual requirement could rise to $420 billion by 2035 after accounting for inflation, the United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP) Adaptation Gap Report 2026 said. Tripling international public adaptation finance could raise annual flows to $85-120 billion by 2035. Including domestic public finance could take the total to $154-189 billion, still leaving more than half of estimated needs unmet. The $305 billion estimate draws on national climate commitments and adaptation plans, alongside modelling studies. It largely covers public and mixed activities, excluding most private-sector requirements, which could add another $260 billion annually in the 2030s. Least developed countries (LDCs) and small island developing states (SIDS) together need an estimated $49-51 billion annually. Low-income countries may need to spend around 4 per cent of their gross domestic product on adaptation.

title: Daily weather tracker: Heavy rain in five southern regions, snowfall in Himalayas and showers in Delhi-NCR
content: Cyclone Murasu has weakened into a low-pressure area over eastern Telangana and coastal Andhra Pradesh, but rainfall is expected to continue across southern India. IMD issues yellow alerts for coastal Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal, warning of isolated heavy rainfall of up to 115.5mm. A western disturbance is likely to bring rain to Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Jammu and Kashmir, with snowfall possible at higher elevations. Delhi-NCR may experience cloudy skies and light showers, with temperatures expected to range between 17°C and 31°C. Several Uttar Pradesh districts face light to moderate rainfall and gusty winds reaching 40km/h. Heavy rain and thunderstorms are forecast across southern India on November 5, while parts of the Himalayan region could receive fresh snowfall, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD). Delhi-NCR and several districts of Uttar Pradesh may also experience light showers and gusty winds as a western disturbance affects northern India. The IMD said the remnants of severe Cyclone Murasu had weakened into a low-pressure area over eastern Telangana and adjoining coastal Andhra Pradesh. Despite weakening, the system is expected to bring further rainfall to neighbouring regions.
